items: Contrast declarative vs imperative infrastructure and explain immutable infrastructure.
Compare Terraform, AWS CloudFormation, and Pulumi in terms of model and portability.
Define GitOps and explain the roles of ArgoCD and Flux.
Explain drift detection and why it matters for compliance.
Sketch a GitOps delivery pipeline from commit to cluster reconciliation.
Infrastructure as Code (IaC) — managing infrastructure through machine-readable definition files, not manual clicks.
Declarative — you state the desired end state; the tool computes the diff (Terraform, CloudFormation).
Imperative — you script the sequence of actions to reach a state.
Immutable infrastructure — never mutate running servers; replace them with new versions.
GitOps — Git is the single source of truth; a controller reconciles cluster state to Git.
Drift — divergence between declared state and actual state.

blocks.text: IaC replaces manual console configuration with versioned files, enabling code review, rollback, and reproducibility. Declarative tools (Terraform, CloudFormation, Pulumi's declarative mode) let you describe the target topology; the engine plans and applies changes. Imperative approaches (raw CLI scripts, Ansible ad-hoc) describe steps. Declarative is preferred for environments because it enables planning and idempotence.

items: Terraform — open-source, multi-cloud, HCL language, large provider ecosystem; state file tracks resources.
CloudFormation — AWS-native, YAML/JSON, tight IAM integration, no state file to manage externally.
Pulumi — uses general-purpose languages (TypeScript, Python, Go); great for developers, same multi-cloud reach.

blocks.text: Instead of patching a live VM, you build a new image (with the patch) and swap it. This eliminates configuration drift, makes rollbacks trivial (redeploy old image), and improves auditability. Containers and VM images (Packer) are the typical vehicles.

GitOps extends IaC: Git holds the desired cluster state (manifests, Helm charts). A controller running in the cluster — ArgoCD or Flux — continuously compares live state to Git and reconciles, pulling changes. This gives auditability (every change is a commit), easy rollback (revert the commit), and closed-loop automation.

Drift happens when someone manually changes infra or an external process alters it. Terraform's plan shows drift; CloudFormation drift detection and ArgoCD's OutOfSync status surface it. GitOps controllers can auto-heal by re-applying desired state, which is essential for compliance and security posture.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Dev as Developer
    participant Git as Git Repo
    participant Ctrl as ArgoCD/Flux
    participant K8s as Kubernetes Cluster
    Dev->>Git: Push manifest change
    Git-->>Ctrl: Webhook / Poll
    Ctrl->>K8s: Reconcile (apply desired state)
    K8s-->>Ctrl: Report actual state
    Ctrl->>Ctrl: Detect drift -> auto-heal
